title: Sudhana's pilgrimage
hookLine: a young seeker visits fifty-three teachers, among them a monk, a girl, a sailor and a king (Flower Garland, Gandavyuha)

cards: Who taught you the thing you actually live by? Not the answer you'd put on a form; the real one.

Sometimes it's somebody nobody would have hired as a teacher: a grandmother, a coach, a bus driver, the kid at the next desk. A long section of the Flower Garland Sutra, called the Gandavyuha, is built on that surprise.
A young man named Sudhana, the seeker carved on the walls of Borobudur, wants to learn how a bodhisattva lives. Instead of settling with one master, he sets off walking.

teach.b: It begins with Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. He sees how much Sudhana wants to learn, and he doesn't hand him the whole teaching.
He tells him to go and find good friends, spiritual friends, and to ask each one how to follow the bodhisattva's way. Then he points him to the first. So Sudhana walks.
And his teachers aren't who you'd expect. There's a monk, yes.

teach.h: A MONK, A GIRL, A SAILOR, A KING.
teach.b: There's also a sailor who knows the sea and its dangers, a girl, laywomen and householders, a perfume seller, a boy, a king. Some are calm and gentle.
A few are startling, and Sudhana has to wonder whether he's come to the right place. Tradition counts fifty-three of them. The same pattern repeats, teacher after teacher.
The teacher tells him what they know: one practice, one door into the way, opened as far as they've opened it. Then, more or less: this is the door I know. I can't tell you about the rest.
Go on to the next. However great the teacher, nobody keeps him, and nobody claims to have the whole of it. Wisdom isn't stored in one well-known person on one mountain.
It's spread out, a piece in a harbor, a piece in a palace, a piece in a shop.
Sudhana's whole job is to keep walking, keep asking, and bow to whoever is standing in front of him.
The next teacher might be the person about to be hurried past.

how: In East Asian Buddhism, Sudhana's journey is told as a model of seeking good spiritual friends, and his meetings with his teachers have been painted and carved in temples.

games.q: you're Sudhana. a teacher has just shown you everything they know. what do they tell you next?
o: stay here, you've found your master.
this is my one door. go on to the next.
games.why: every teacher says some version of it: this is the door I know. go on. nobody keeps him, and nobody claims the whole.

practice: Let a memory come of someone who taught you something without meaning to: a stranger on a train, a remark from a coworker, a sentence overheard in a waiting room.
Stay with that moment and ask what door they opened that you hadn't found. Then leave the question open, the way Sudhana kept walking.

wordCard.voice: Sudhana's pilgrimage. A young seeker's long walk from teacher to teacher in the Flower Garland Sutra, each one knowing a single door. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a good friend, a spiritual friend. the kind of teacher Sudhana is sent to find.

carryVoice: Your line: fifty-three teachers. None of them was the last stop on the road. See you tomorrow.
